Snow to Snow

On June 7 I started the morning in snow at Arapahoe Basin and spent the afternoon on an e-bike beside Lake Dillon, with snowy peaks across the water. It was one of a handful of day trips squeezed in around family life that year. I'd first gone up to the Basin on May 22, a flat gray day with the whole bowl still white. A-Basin is known for holding its snow long after everyone else has put the skis away. Back up on the 7th, the sky was clear blue and crossed by contrails, and brown tundra had begun to show through the ski tracks along the ridge.

By the end of September the gold had arrived. On the 28th I caught the last light near Bailey, where a whole hillside of aspens glowed between pockets of dark spruce. The grass at my feet looked frosted, and beyond it a wide basin faded off to layered blue ranges under a peach and pink sky. Eight days later I was beside a creek near Georgetown, and the show was nearly over. The trunks stood bare and chalky white, with one young aspen holding on to its yellow-green leaves. The mountains don't check with me first. All I can do is show up and hope I'm on time.

Then the snow came back. On the morning of November 4, I-70 near Idaho Springs was wet and gray, with fresh snow flocking the conifers and frosting the cliffs. The toll express lane was marked closed. By noon, near Keystone, the new snow had found its best audience: a dog who rolled around in it until there was more snow than dog. On December 15 I was high on the ski mountain at Keystone on a clear afternoon, with wind streaming snow off a broad white summit. From late snow in spring to fresh snow in winter, none of it needed a plane ticket.
